Motion Planning via Optimal Transport

The problem: trajectory optimization gives smooth robot motions, but it needs cost-function gradients that often don't exist (occupancy maps, contacts), and it gets trapped in local minima. The trick (Le et al., NeurIPS 2023): around every waypoint of a batch of trajectories, probe the cost along the vertices of a regular polytope, then let a tiny optimal-transport problem — solved by Sinkhorn's algorithm — "transport" each waypoint toward the cheap directions. One update, no gradients, thousands of waypoints at once on a GPU. This page builds the method from scratch: optimal transport → the Sinkhorn Step update rule → why it converges → how it becomes a motion planner → what the experiments say.

Source: A. Le, G. Chalvatzaki, A. Biess, J. Peters, “Accelerating Motion Planning via Optimal Transport”, NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2309.15970). Code name: MPOT; update rule: Sinkhorn Step.

1 · Why 2 · Optimal transport 3 · Sinkhorn Step 4 · Convergence 5 · Planning as inference 6 · The MPOT loop 7 · Experiments 8 · Context

1. The problem: move a trajectory when you can't differentiate

A robot motion is a discrete trajectory \(\tau = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_T)\) — waypoints in configuration space with \(x_0\) the start. Trajectory optimization searches for the \(\tau\) that minimizes a sum of planning costs:

\[ \tau^{*} \;=\; \arg\min_{\tau}\;\Big[ c_{\mathrm{obs}}(\tau) + c_{g}(\tau, x_{g}) + c_{\mathrm{sm}}(\tau) \Big] \qquad \text{s.t. } \dot{x} = f(x,u),\; x_0 \text{ given} \]

with an obstacle cost \(c_{\mathrm{obs}}\), a goal cost \(c_g\) pulling the end of the trajectory to \(x_g\), and a smoothness cost \(c_{\mathrm{sm}}\) so the low-level controller can actually track the plan. Every serious motion planner must handle three hard facts about this problem:

  • The landscape is non-convex and multi-modal. A cluttered room admits several homotopy classes — go left of the table or right — separated by high-cost walls. A single optimizer run picks one basin, and gradient descent descends straight into whichever basin it started in, often a bad one.
  • Gradients are often unavailable or lie. If the environment is given as an occupancy map (a grid of occupied/free cells — the standard representation from a lidar or a voxel map), the obstacle cost is a step function: its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at cell boundaries. The same happens with contact and torque-limit costs. Gradient-based planners such as CHOMP or GPMP2 instead need a signed distance field, which must be crafted or learned for the scene.
  • Batch parallelism breaks classical step sizes. Modern GPUs let you optimize hundreds of trajectories at once — which is how you cover multiple modes and harvest diverse solutions for learning pipelines. But a shared gradient step size that is safe for one trajectory is often unstable for another (CHOMP's known failure in narrow passages under parallelization).

The paper's answer is a zero-order update rule — it evaluates costs, never derivatives — that updates every waypoint of every trajectory independently, with a step whose size is bounded by construction, and that is one matrix operation on a GPU. The machinery that makes "evaluate locally, then move" principled instead of heuristic is entropic optimal transport, so we build that first.

Takeaway: trajectory optimization needs a derivative-free, batch-capable, provably-descending waypoint update — that is exactly the role the Sinkhorn Step will play.

2. Entropic optimal transport in three small steps

2.1 Moving mass at minimum cost

Optimal transport (OT) asks: given a pile of mass at some origins and a demand at some destinations, what is the cheapest way to ship it? In the discrete case the pile is a histogram \(n \in \Sigma_n\) — a non-negative vector summing to one, \(\Sigma_d := \{x \in \mathbb{R}^d_{+} : x^\top \mathbf{1}_d = 1\}\) — and likewise \(m \in \Sigma_m\). A transport plan is a matrix \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}_{+}\) whose row sums are \(n\), column sums \(m\):

\[ U(n,m) \;=\; \{ W \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}_{+} \;:\; W\mathbf{1}_m = n,\; W^\top \mathbf{1}_n = m \} \]

Entry \(W_{ij}\) is "how much mass moves from origin \(i\) to destination \(j\)". With a cost matrix \(C \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}_{+}\) (unit shipping cost from \(i\) to \(j\)), classic OT is the linear program

\[ \mathrm{OT}(n,m) \;=\; \min_{W \in U(n,m)} \langle W, C \rangle \;=\; \min_{W}\; \sum_{i,j} W_{ij} C_{ij}. \]

Exact OT is expensive at scale, so Cuturi (2013) added an entropy bonus that keeps the plan spread out and makes the problem strictly convex and solvable by a few matrix–vector products:

\[ \mathrm{OT}_{\lambda}(n,m) \;=\; \min_{W \in U(n,m)}\; \langle W, C\rangle - \lambda\, H(W) \qquad\text{with } H(W) = -\!\!\sum_{i,j} W_{ij}\log W_{ij}. \tag{1} \]

Large \(\lambda\) → plan is blurry (entropy wins); \(\lambda \to 0\) → recovers the exact LP.

2.2 Sinkhorn's algorithm: two renormalizations in a loop

Problem (1) has a beautiful structure: its optimum has the form \(W^{*}_{ij} = u_i\, P_{ij}\, v_j\) with the Gibbs kernel \(P_{ij} = e^{-C_{ij}/\lambda}\) and two positive vectors \(u, v\). Finding \(u,v\) so that the marginals match is a fixed point of two alternating normalizations — the Sinkhorn (a.k.a. Sinkhorn-Knopp) iterations:

\[ u^{(i+1)} = \frac{n}{P\,v^{(i)}}, \qquad v^{(i+1)} = \frac{m}{P^{\top} u^{(i+1)}}, \qquad W^{*}_{\lambda} = \operatorname{diag}(u)\, P\, \operatorname{diag}(v). \tag{2} \]

Each pass rescales rows to match \(n\), then columns to match \(m\), then rows again; convergence is geometric. In practice one runs it in the log domain (absorbing huge factors \(u = \tilde{u}\,e^{a/\lambda}\) into log-space offsets \(a\)) because small \(\lambda\) makes \(e^{-C/\lambda}\) underflow — the paper uses exactly this stabilization (its Appendix E).

Intuition: Sinkhorn is just "row-normalize, column-normalize, repeat" on the kernel \(e^{-C/\lambda}\). The entropy term is what makes the two normalizations compatible — without it, hard marginals can be unachievable and the LP needs a combinatorial solver.

2.3 A worked 2×2 example

Take two origins, two destinations, unit marginals \((\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\), and cost matrix \(C = \big(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\big)\). Origin 1 would rather ship to destination 1 (\(1 < 4\)); origin 2 to destination 2 (\(1 < 2\)). Run the iterations (2):

\(\lambda\)\(W^{*}_{\lambda}\)behavior
\(0.1\) \(\big(\begin{smallmatrix} 0.500 & 0.000 \\ 0.000 & 0.500 \end{smallmatrix}\big)\) nearly the exact LP: a soft assignment — each origin picks its cheap destination
\(1.0\) \(\big(\begin{smallmatrix} 0.440 & 0.060 \\ 0.060 & 0.440 \end{smallmatrix}\big)\) blurry: every entry gets some mass; the plan is a smoothed compromise

Two observations matter for what follows. First, at small \(\lambda\) the plan is a soft permutation — OT is secretly an assignment algorithm. Second, the column marginals are hard: each destination receives exactly total mass \(m_j\) no matter what. This "every destination gets served" property will become "every search direction gets used" — the source of the method's unbiasedness. (Both numbers above were verified by an independent Sinkhorn implementation for this page.)

Takeaway: entropic OT turns a cost matrix into a soft assignment of rows to columns, computed by cheap convergent iterations — with hard column marginals and tunable softness \(\lambda\).

3. The Sinkhorn Step: transport your parameters downhill

3.1 The setup

Now switch hats: instead of shipping goods, we are minimizing a non-convex, \(L\)-smooth, bounded-below function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) (Assumption 1 of the paper) over a batch of \(n\) points \(X_k = \{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\), with function values cheap and derivatives expensive or unavailable. We want a batch update rule with three properties:

  1. every point can, over several steps, reach any point of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (no forbidden directions);
  2. the step is provably descent-like for small enough step size;
  3. the whole batch updates in one vectorized operation.

3.2 Search directions from regular polytopes

Center a regular polytope on each point: the \(d\)-simplex (\(d{+}1\) vertices), the \(d\)-orthoplex (\(2d\) vertices, the generalized octahedron), or the \(d\)-cube (\(2^d\) vertices), each inscribed in the unit sphere \(\mathcal{S}^{d-1}\). The unit vertex vectors \(\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}} = \{d_1,\dots,d_m\}\) have two key properties:

  • They are unbiased: \(\sum_i d_i = 0\) — no direction is privileged;
  • They positively span \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (Proposition 1): every \(v \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is a non-negative combination \(\sum_i w_i d_i\), \(w_i \ge 0\). So a sequence of steps along polytope directions can reach anything — including, crucially, the descent direction.
2-simplex \(m = 3\) 2-cube (= 2-orthoplex) \(m = 4\) worst case: bisects two vertices (\(\cos = \mu_{\mathcal P}\)) one waypoint, randomly rotated 2-cube \(x_t\) ● probe points (per direction) \(C_{t,i}=1.2\) \(C_{t,i}=0.0\) \(C_{t,i}=0.1\) \(C_{t,i}=0.9\) ⟶ update = barycenter of cheap vertices
Figure 1. Left: the two planar members of the regular-polytope family inscribed in the unit sphere. Both positively span the plane; for any vector \(a\) there is always a vertex \(d\) with \(\langle a, d\rangle \ge \mu_{\mathcal{P}}\lVert a\rVert\) — the cosine measure \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\) is attained when \(a\) bisects two adjacent vertices. Right: the local probing of one waypoint (paper's Fig. 2): a randomly rotated 2-cube gives 4 directions; \(h\) probe points are placed along each direction between the step radius \(\alpha_k\) (solid circle) and the probe radius \(\beta_k \ge \alpha_k\) (dashed circle); the per-direction mean cost \(C_{t,i}\) feeds the OT, and the waypoint is transported toward the barycenter of the cheap vertices (blue arrow).

The worst-case alignment between any vector \(a\) (in particular \(-\nabla f\)) and the best polytope vertex is quantified by the cosine measure (Lemma 1):

\[ \exists\, d \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{P}}:\quad \langle a, d\rangle \;\ge\; \mu_{\mathcal{P}}\, \lVert a \rVert, \qquad \mu_{\mathcal{P}} = \begin{cases} 1/\sqrt{d(d+1)} & d\text{-simplex}\\[2pt] 1/\sqrt{d} & d\text{-orthoplex}\\[2pt] 1/\sqrt{2}\;\;(\text{const.}) & d\text{-cube} \end{cases} \]

\(\mu_{\mathcal P}\) is a guarantee: even in the unluckiest orientation, one of the \(m\) probes aligns with the negative gradient at least to cosine \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\). Buying a bigger \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\) costs more vertices per iteration: \(d{+}1\), \(2d\), or \(2^d\) cost evaluations.

3.3 The update rule

Now the punchline of the paper (Definition 2). At iteration \(k\), with step size \(\alpha_k\):

\[ X_{k+1} \;=\; X_k + S_k, \qquad S_k \;=\; \alpha_k\, \operatorname{diag}(n)^{-1} W^{*}_{\lambda}\, D_{\mathcal{P}}, \qquad C_{ij} = f\!\big(x_i + \alpha_k d_j\big) \tag{4} \]

Read it from the inside out:

  1. Probe. Translate the polytope to each point \(x_i\) and evaluate \(f\) at its (scaled) vertices: row \(i\) of \(C\) is the local cost landscape sampled on \(m\) compass points around \(x_i\).
  2. Transport. Solve the entropic OT between the histogram over points \(n \in \Sigma_n\) and the histogram over directions \(m \in \Sigma_m\). The plan \(W^{*}_{\lambda}\) is \(n \times m\): a soft assignment of points to directions, globally forced to use every direction with total mass \(m_j\).
  3. Move. \(\operatorname{diag}(n)^{-1}W^{*}_{\lambda}\) normalizes each row into a probability vector over directions (a barycentric coordinate). Each point steps by \(\alpha_k\) times the weighted average of the unit vertices — a point inside the polytope's convex hull, scaled by \(\alpha_k\).

In free-support OT language (Cuturi & Doucet 2014), the new point is the barycentric projection of the old one under the optimal plan: the points are the "mass", the polytope vertices are the "destinations", and the cost matrix decides which destinations are cheap. In directional-search language, it is a soft, batched pattern-search step: classical direct search would take \(\arg\min_j C_{ij}\); entropic OT replaces the argmin with a \(\lambda\)-controlled softmax-like weighting while keeping the marginals hard.

Intuition: why OT, and not just a softmax over the \(m\) costs? A per-point softmax would let every point crowd onto the single cheapest direction. The column marginals of OT forbid that: in total, each direction must carry \(1/m\) of the mass. The update is therefore a globally balanced, compromise-free matching between "who wants to go where" — which is precisely what keeps a batch of points spread out instead of collapsing, and what makes the step a transport problem rather than a per-point one.

A second gift of the formulation is an explicit trust region. Since each row of \(\operatorname{diag}(n)^{-1}W^{*}_{\lambda}\) is a convex combination of unit vertices, the step lies in the polytope hull: \(\lVert s_i\rVert \le \alpha_k\) — no matter what the costs say (paper's Appendix D). Gradient methods get their trust region from a regularized Taylor expansion; here the geometry of the probe set is the trust region, which is why one shared \(\alpha_k\) is safe for a whole heterogeneous batch. With \(\lambda = 0.01\) (the paper's setting) the plan is nearly a permutation, so points take nearly the full step toward their best vertex, with a small entropy-induced shrinking toward the centroid.

3.4 The mechanism in one dimension

The figure below is a live run of Definition 2 that I implemented for this page: \(f(x) = 0.1x^2 + 1.1\sin(2.2x)\) — non-convex, four wells — a batch of 14 points, the 1-cube directions \(\{-1,+1\}\), \(\alpha = 0.3\), \(\beta = 0.85\), \(h = 6\) probes, \(\lambda = 0.05\). No derivatives anywhere.

Figure 2. Sinkhorn Step on a 1-D non-convex cost (green triangles: local minima). Each point probes both sides (blue arrows show one update), the OT plan softly assigns points to their cheaper side — with the side-marginals balanced globally — and the batch self-organizes into the wells. After 15 steps every point sits in a minimum basin; no gradient was computed.

Notice what the balanced transport did not do: it did not drag all points to the same global minimum. Points far apart have different cost rows, so the plan assigns them differently; the marginals only enforce that, in total, left-moves and right-moves are used equally. Diversity of the batch survives — which is exactly what the planner will exploit.

Takeaway: the Sinkhorn Step = probe the cost on a local polytope → solve one entropic OT → move each point to the barycenter of its cheap vertices. It is a trust-region method whose trust region is drawn by geometry, not by calculus.

4. Why it converges: the descent inequality

The paper connects the Sinkhorn Step to directional direct search (the Hooke–Jeeves/pattern-search family). Under Assumption 2 (uniform histograms with \(n = m\), and \(\lambda \to 0\)), Birkhoff's theorem says the extreme points of \(U(n,m)\) are permutation matrices — the soft assignment hardens into a bijection between points and directions — and each point's step reduces to the classical direct-search step "go to your best vertex". Two cases cover the limit: the plan is a permutation, or a convex combination of tied optimal permutations; in both, the step \(s_k\) is a weighted combination of descending steps.

Combine this with the guarantee that some vertex aligns with the negative gradient to cosine \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\) (Lemma 1), and with the \(L\)-smoothness bound \(f(x+s) \le f(x) + \langle\nabla f, s\rangle + \tfrac{L}{2}\lVert s\rVert^2\) (valid for any step \(s\)). Because \(\lVert s_k\rVert \le \alpha_k\), every point separately obeys the key descent inequality (Lemma 2):

\[ f(x_{k+1}) \;\le\; f(x_k) \;-\; \mu_{\mathcal{P}}\,\alpha_k \lVert \nabla f(x_k)\rVert \;+\; \frac{L}{2}\,\alpha_k^{2}. \tag{12} \]
Intuition — read (12) as a tug-of-war. First term: a real descent of order \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\alpha\lVert\nabla f\rVert\) — the guaranteed alignment of the best vertex with the descent direction, times the step length. Second term: the universal "curvature tax" \(\tfrac{L}{2}\alpha^2\) — the most any \(L\)-smooth function can bite you for moving a distance \(\alpha\). While \(\lVert\nabla f\rVert\) is large the descent term wins and the cost falls; the tax is what stops you from overshooting into a valley wall.

Telescoping (12) over \(K\) steps and using \(f \ge f^{*}\) gives the main theorem (Theorem 1): if the step is small enough, \(\alpha < 2\mu_{\mathcal P}\epsilon/L\), then after

\[ K \;\ge\; k(\epsilon) \;=\; \frac{f(x_0) - f^{*}}{(\mu_{\mathcal P}\,\epsilon - \tfrac{L}{2}\alpha^{2})\,\alpha} \;-\; 1 \] steps, some iterate satisfies \(\min_{0\le k\le K}\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert \le \epsilon\).

Choosing the optimal step \(\alpha = \mu_{\mathcal P}\epsilon/L\) yields the complexity \(k(\epsilon) = 2L(f(x_0)-f^{*})/(\mu_{\mathcal P}^2\epsilon^2) - 1\), and plugging in each polytope's \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\) (Remark 1):

polytopevertices \(m\)\(\mu_{\mathcal P}\)iterations to \(\epsilon\)-stationaritycost evals per iter.
\(d\)-simplex\(d{+}1\)\(1/\sqrt{d(d{+}1)}\)\(\mathcal{O}(d^2/\epsilon^2)\)\(d{+}1\)
\(d\)-orthoplex\(2d\)\(1/\sqrt{d}\)\(\mathcal{O}(d/\epsilon^2)\)\(2d\)
\(d\)-cube\(2^d\)\(1/\sqrt{2}\)\(\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)\)\(2^d\)

The \(d\)-cube matches gradient descent's famous \(\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)\) — but pays \(2^d\) evaluations per step, so it is only practical for small \(d\). The orthoplex is the workhorse for high \(d\): \(\mathcal{O}(d/\epsilon^2)\) iterations at \(2d\) evaluations each. Note the honest caveat the authors attach: the guarantee is that some iterate enters the \(\epsilon\)-stationary set; enforcing monotone descent via a sufficient-decrease check \(f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1}) \ge c\alpha_k^2\) would upgrade "some" to "the last", but wastes iterations in practice — and the experiments show convergence without it.

Takeaway: the Sinkhorn Step inherits pattern-search convergence: descent rate proportional to the cosine measure \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\), with \(\mathcal{O}(d/\epsilon^2)\) iterations for the orthoplex and gradient-descent-grade \(\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)\) for the cube.

5. From parameter vectors to trajectories: planning as inference

The Sinkhorn Step updates independent points. A trajectory is not a bag of independent points — its waypoints are glued together by dynamics and smoothness. The paper's bridge is the planning-as-inference view, which turns "smooth, dynamically feasible trajectory" into a cost term that the waypoint-wise update can carry.

5.1 The posterior over trajectories

Give trajectories a prior — a zero-mean Gaussian process \(q_F(\tau) = \mathcal{N}(0, K)\) built from a constant-velocity stochastic dynamics (white-noise acceleration), discretized at \(\Delta t\). Its precision is sparse: \(K^{-1} = D^\top Q^{-1} D\) with \(D\) a block first-difference matrix, so the prior density factors over pairs of neighboring waypoints (paper's Appendix B):

\[ q_F(\tau) \;\propto\; q_s(x_0)\, q_g(x_T) \prod_{t=0}^{T-1} \underbrace{\exp\!\Big[-\tfrac12 \big\lVert \Phi_{t,t+1}(x_t - \mu_t) - (x_{t+1}-\mu_{t+1}) \big\rVert^2_{Q_{t,t+1}^{-1}}\Big]}_{\text{binary GP factor}} \]

\(\Phi_{t,t+1}\) is the constant-velocity state transition and \(Q_{t,t+1}\) the integrated process noise. Then define the target posterior as cost-tempered prior:

\[ q^{*}(\tau) \;=\; \frac{1}{Z}\,\exp\big(-\eta\, c(\tau)\big)\; q_F(\tau) \tag{7} \]

\(\eta\) is an inverse temperature. Planning as inference means: find the most probable trajectory, i.e. minimize some divergence between a proposal and \(q^{*}\).

5.2 The I-projection gives a classical planning objective

The trajectory is represented by its waypoint empirical distribution \(p(x;\tau) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{T}\,\delta_{x_t}(x)\) (Eq. 8) — a histogram with one atom per waypoint. Projecting it onto \(q^{*}\) in KL (the I-projection, Eq. 9) and dropping constants (\(H(p) = \log T\) is fixed for a fixed \(T\)) yields:

\[ \tau^{*} = \arg\min_{\tau}\; \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\; \Big[\; \underbrace{\eta\, c(x_t)}_{\text{state cost}} \;+\; \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\big\lVert \Phi_{t,t+1}\,x_t - x_{t+1}\big\rVert^{2}_{Q_{t,t+1}^{-1}}}_{\text{transition (smoothness) cost}} \Big] \tag{9} \]

This is exactly the classical trajectory-optimization objective (2) — the GP prior did not add machinery, it became the smoothness cost. That is the whole point of the inference detour: smoothness enters as pairwise costs between neighbors, not as a matrix to invert, and — crucially for us — not as something that needs gradients propagated through a kinematic chain. (Compared to GPMP2's moment projection, the paper's I-projection also removes the importance-sampling step: the model lives in the cost, the update acts directly on waypoint parameters.)

5.3 Feeding Eq. (9) to the Sinkhorn Step

The objective (9) is a sum over waypoints of a state cost plus a term coupling each waypoint to its neighbor. To probe it locally at waypoint \(t\), the paper places \(h\) points \(y_{t,i,j}\) along direction \(i\) out to radius \(\beta_k \ge \alpha_k\), and prices direction \(i\) by the mean cost-to-go over the probes (Eq. 10):

\[ C_{t,i} \;=\; \frac{1}{h}\sum_{j=1}^{h}\; \Big[\; \eta\, c\big(x_t + y_{t,i,j}\big) \;+\; \tfrac12\big\lVert \Phi_{t,t+1}x_t - (x_{t+1} + y_{t+1,i,j})\big\rVert^{2}_{Q^{-1}_{t,t+1}} \Big] \tag{10} \]

The second term asks: if the neighbor moved along this same direction, how much would the GP link be stretched? It is what keeps the transport smooth — a waypoint's direction is cheap only if it is also compatible with its neighbor moving consistently. Each waypoint gets its own randomly rotated polytope \(R \in SO(d)\), sampled fresh every iteration: this de-biases the probe geometry (a fixed polytope would systematically miss features oriented between vertices) and decorrelates the rows of the cost matrix. All \(T\) waypoints of all \(N_p\) trajectories are flattened into one batch of \(N = N_p \cdot T\) points; one \(\mathbb{R}^{N \times m}\) OT instance updates them all.

And the trust region? Flattening Eq. (25) of the paper: since every row of the plan is a convex combination of unit vertices,

\[ \lVert \tau_{k+1} - \tau_k \rVert \;\le\; T\,\alpha_k \qquad\text{— a bound that does not depend on the costs at all.} \]
Intuition: smoothness without a single derivative. The state cost \(c\) may be a raw occupancy lookup — a step function. Nobody differentiates it; it is only sampled at probe points. The smoothness that low-level controllers need comes from the GP link, which prices candidate moves by how much they would tear the trajectory's neighborhood apart. Gradient-free state costs + pairwise smoothness = the MPOT recipe.

5.4 The demo: two goals, one wall, no gradients

Figure 3. A run of the full pipeline simulated for this page: 12 trajectories (6 per goal, gold stars) × 24 waypoints = 288 points updated jointly by one \(\mathbb{R}^{288\times 4}\) Sinkhorn Step per iteration; randomly rotated 2-cubes, \(h=5\) probes per direction, binary (inflated) occupancy cost, GP-style neighbor coupling, \(\lambda = 0.01\), step and probe radii annealed geometrically. Collision-free plans turn blue. The batch discovers both homotopy classes (above and below the wall) while some plans stay stuck — the planner returns the best plan, and the surviving diversity is a feature (multi-modality), not a bug.

Small print, for fidelity: my demo evaluates the GP link on the probe point of the waypoint itself against both neighbors (the symmetric form of Eq. 10 — one link per row is the paper's asymmetric version, and using both is what keeps the toy batch from zig-zagging), and inflates the occupancy radius the way costmaps are conventionally inflated. Neither changes the algorithmic story; both make a 288-point toy stable.

Takeaway: planning-as-inference converts the GP dynamics prior into pairwise smoothness costs, so the whole planning objective is probe-able — and the Sinkhorn Step can optimize a batch of trajectories over even non-differentiable state costs.

6. The MPOT loop in practice

Assembled end-to-end, the planner is short (paper's Algorithm 1):

// initialization: GP prior = straight line + exploratory covariance
T⁰ ~ N(μ₀, K₀) // μ₀: constant-velocity line start→goal, K₀: large GP covariance
n = 1_N / N, m = 1_m / m
while not converged:
  (optional) α ← (1−ϵ)·α, β ← (1−ϵ)·β // anneal trust region
  build randomly rotated D_P ∈ R^{N×m×d}, probe set H_P ∈ R^{N×m×h×d}; evaluate C (Eq. 10)
  C ← C − min(C) // positivity for numerical stability
  W* ← stabilized Sinkhorn(C, n, m, λ = 0.01) // log-domain (paper's Alg. 2)
  T ← T + α·diag(n)⁻¹·W*·D_P // one Sinkhorn Step, all waypoints at once
return argmin over trajectories of the planning cost

Four practical details carry real weight:

  • Initialization is part of the algorithm. Trajectories are sampled from a constant-velocity GP prior centered on the straight line start→goal with large covariance: cheap, smooth, and diverse — Figure 3's panel "step 0". The prior, not the update, is what injects multi-modality.
  • Log-domain Sinkhorn. With \(N\) in the thousands and \(\lambda = 0.01\), the kernel \(e^{-C/\lambda}\) underflows. The stabilized algorithm reparameterizes \(u = \tilde u\, e^{a/\lambda}\), \(v = \tilde v\, e^{b/\lambda}\) and computes \(P^{(i)}_{tj} = \exp\big((a_t + b_j - C_{tj})/\lambda\big)\) so extremes cancel before exponentiation. This keeps each inner solve at a few matrix products.
  • Annealing = explore, then exploit. Since \(L\) is unknown, the optimal step \(\alpha = \mu_{\mathcal P}\epsilon/L\) cannot be computed; without annealing the iterate oscillates around a minimum. Shrinking \(\alpha_k, \beta_k\) by a factor \((1-\epsilon)\) per step trades a bit of escape ability for sharp convergence — the ablation (§7) quantifies exactly this trade.
  • Later iterations solve OT faster. As waypoints settle, the cost rows become more uniform, and the inner Sinkhorn loop terminates in 1–2 iterations instead of dozens — the planner accelerates as it converges (paper's Fig. 3).
Figure 4. The demo run of Figure 3, measured. Left: mean planning cost over the batch decays steadily across 110 Sinkhorn Steps. Right: the geometric annealing schedules of the step radius \(\alpha_k\) (0.55 → 0.12) and probe radius \(\beta_k\) (1.4 → 0.8) — the trust region tightens as the batch converges, mirroring the paper's ϵ-annealing.
Takeaway: MPOT = GP-prior initialization + probe/OT/update loop + log-domain Sinkhorn + radius annealing. Every ingredient exists to keep the one big batched update stable without gradients.

7. Does it work? The experiments

The paper benchmarks against gradient-based planners (CHOMP, GPMP2), gradient-free stochastic ones (STOMP, SGPMP), and the sampling-based gold standards RRT*/Informed-RRT*, all reimplemented in PyTorch and tuned per environment. Metrics: planning time \(T[s]\) to convergence; task success \(\mathrm{SUC}[\%]\) (≥1 collision-free plan per task); parallelization quality \(\mathrm{GOOD}[\%]\) (fraction of the batch that succeeds); smoothness \(S\) (mean velocity jump) and path length \(PL\).

How to read this. RRT\(^*\) always eventually succeeds (probabilistic completeness) but takes 40–190 s — useless for real-time, and its raw paths need post-smoothing. CHOMP is fast but fails in narrow passages: with a whole batch sharing one step size, the size that is stable for the majority overshoots the few trajectories squeezed through gaps. STOMP's Gaussian sampling variance can't produce the sharp turns dense clutter demands. SGPMP matches success rates but pays for its proposal-based updates with 6.5 s. MPOT wins time (0.4 s / 0.8 s — ~4–8× faster than the best competitor) while matching or beating success, because (i) waypoints update independently, so narrow-passage trajectories are not hostage to the batch's shared step size, and (ii) the explicit trust region makes one \(\alpha_k\) safe for everyone.

The high-dimensional stress test: 36-DoF mobile manipulation

The TIAGo++ task — navigate, fetch a cup, place it on a shelf, avoid chairs — is one planning problem per phase with 128 timesteps and \(d = 36\) (base + torso + two 7-DoF arms). SDFs are painful to craft here, whole-body IK is unreliable, and RRT\(^*\) fails outright within a 1000 s budget:

An 11–27× speedup at the highest success rate. The one blemish is honest and instructive: MPOT's smoothness \(S\) and path length \(PL\) are the worst of the successful planners here, because in \(d = 36\) the orthoplex's \(m = 72\) directions are a very sparse sample of the sphere — the trust region is boxy, and smoothing must be traded against success when tuning. Sparsity of the direction set is the price of gradient-freedom at high dimension.

Ablations: each design choice earns its keep

  • Random rotation (paper Fig. 7): removing it — same polytopes, fixed orientation — degrades the cost approximation badly (biased probes), and more so in higher dimensions.
  • Annealing: disabling it converges slower but finds more successful local minima (~80% vs ~74% GOOD in the point-mass ablation): a wide trust region escapes basins that a tightened one cannot. Speed vs. coverage is a dial, not a bug.
  • Polytope choice (paper Table 5, Panda): orthoplex 0.8 s / 71.6% SUC; simplex 0.5 s / 65.8% (faster, sparser, less reliable); uniformly random sphere points 2.5 s / 70.1% with worse smoothness — polytope structure, not just direction count, is what makes the OT well-conditioned.
  • \(\lambda\) and the gradient connection (paper Fig. 10): on a smooth test function, the cosine similarity between the Sinkhorn Step direction and the true negative gradient rises with \(\mu_{\mathcal P}\) (cube > orthoplex > simplex, exactly as Lemma 1 predicts) and with larger \(\lambda\) — the entropic blur acts as a smoothing regularizer on the direction estimate.
Takeaway: across 2-D to 36-D tasks, MPOT trades gradients for probing and wins on planning time by 4–27× at equal-or-better success; its known weakness is direction-set sparsity in very high dimensions.

8. Where it sits, and what it can't do (yet)

Lineage. The Sinkhorn Step is a hybrid of three classical ideas:

  • Directional direct search (Hooke & Jeeves 1961; positive spanning sets, cosine measures): the polytope probes and the descent analysis of §4 are pattern search with a probabilistic, batched twist.
  • Entropic optimal transport (Sinkhorn–Knopp 1967; Cuturi 2013) and free-support Wasserstein barycenters (Cuturi & Doucet 2014): the update is the barycentric projection of a barycenter problem whose "distributions" are points and polytope vertices.
  • Planning as inference (Toussaint 2009; GPMP/GPMP2; SGPMP): the GP prior enters as pairwise costs (§5), but with the moment-projection/importance-sampling machinery replaced by direct waypoint transport.

Honest limitations (from the paper's own accounting): the entropic OT inner solve can still go numerically unstable for very large \(N\) (log-domain helps; rare divergence remains); the convergence theory assumes \(n = m\) and \(\lambda \to 0\) while the practice runs \(N \gg m\) at \(\lambda = 0.01\) — the analysis is a bridge to the direct-search literature, not a full account of the practical algorithm; and in high dimensions the sparse direction set forces a tune-between-smoothness-and-success compromise. The authors flag natural next steps: learned motion priors as initializers, SVGD-style diversity mechanisms inside the batch, and conditional (per-waypoint) marginals.

When would you reach for this? When costs are natural as evaluations (occupancy grids, simulators, contact checks) but not as derivatives; when you want many diverse, smooth candidate plans in one GPU round (dataset generation for policy learning, multi-modal prediction); or when a shared gradient step size across a batch is the thing breaking your trajectory optimization. If you have clean SDFs and a single well-initialized trajectory, CHOMP/GPMP2 remain excellent.

Takeaway: MPOT = pattern search + Sinkhorn transport + GP inference — a gradient-free batch planner whose real contribution is an update rule: probe a polytope, let balanced transport pick the barycenter, and let geometry draw the trust region.
